newsitem.title: INDIA: Final phase of Kashmir polls begins quietly.
newsitem.headline: Final phase of Kashmir polls begins quietly.

text.p: The final phase of local polls in India's Jammu and Kashmir state began quietly on Monday as the troubled region prepared for the return of democracy after six years of separatist revolt, officials said.

"There are not many people (voting) at the moment, but we expect the pace to pick up during the day," said an election official at Banihal, 95 km (55 miles) south of the state's summer capital Srinagar.
Voting booths opened at 7 a.m. (0130 GMT) and were set to close at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) when the staggered month-long elections would end.
Srinagar's streets were deserted and shops were shut as residents observed a strike called by the separatist All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which opposes the polls.
"We hope things will improve after the elections," said a 23-year-old college student. He said his teachers had not delivered a single lecture during his three-year course.
"They could not dare to defy the militants," he said.
Monday's polls in the mountainous Doda district, 250 km (150 miles) south of Srinagar, were guarded by more than 22,000 paramilitary troopers, election officials said.
"The voting opened on a note of enthusiasm," government spokesman K.B. Jandial told Reuters.
About 300,000 people were eligible to vote for 45 candidates in six of the state's 87 constituencies on Monday.
Many of the guerrilla groups fighting either for independence or merger with Islamic Pakistan have hide-outs in Doda's bleak terrain, police said.

Police said suspected militants fired at Bahujan Samaj Party candidate Jagat Ram on Sunday at Ramban, about 100 km (60 miles) south of Srinagar. He escaped unharmed after his security guard returned the fire.
The federal government in New Delhi has ruled the state directly since 1990, when the state assembly was dissolved after the separatist revolt flared.
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have since died in insurgency-related violence.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government in New Delhi hopes the elections will pave the way for the return of normalcy to the rugged Himalayan region.
The local elections are the first since 1987. The polls were staggered in four phases spread over a month to permit the movement of thousands of security forces and polling staff.

At least 21 people, almost all political activists, have been killed during the campaign. Farooq Abdullah, the leader of the state's biggest party, the National Conference, escaped two grenade attacks.

Election officials said repolling was also underway at 21 stations in some parts of the Moslem-majority Kashmir valley, where voting in earlier phases was disrupted by scattered violence and allegations of coercion by security forces, denied by authorities.
Vote counting was set to start on Tuesday, and initial trends were expected by Wednesday, officials said.
National Conference chief Farooq Abdullah was widely tipped to become the state's new chief minister. He held that post in 1990 when the separatist rebellion broke out.
